title: Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's timetable hung at Muileann chrom
summary: The mended line's copied timetable, carried over from the humans' own working papers, is hung on a board at the Muileann chrom terminus where the rails now end. Passengers and carters read it as they find it, since no one troubles to explain why a six-year-old kingdom keeps a dead people's hours.

title: The talk at the net-mending
summary: Under the eaves of the net-store church at Baile chrom, the winter's net-mending turns to talk of Hannah Crane's word that Oidhche Glaise vigil will be kept in the open. Some call it needless risk to an old office; others say it is overdue. No one carries the talk beyond the town.

title: The old priest's counsel
summary: Walking back from a burial, the priest of Baile chrom tells Hannah Crane that the vigil's keeping is hers to judge, having held his own office forty years by staying out of what belongs to another. It is the only word of encouragement she has from anyone before the night.

title: The maor's man watches and writes nothing
summary: A clerk's assistant of Cnoc ghorm, lodging at Baile chrom on an unrelated errand, climbs a rise above the headland and watches Hannah Crane's vigil through the night from a distance. He carries no instruction to report it and no form to record it on, and the shire's returns for the week say nothing.

title: The bishops' letter kept behind the altar-cloth
summary: Three bishops of An Eaglais write to Baile chrom calling the open keeping of Oidhche Glaise irregular, and ask, without commanding, that the custom be given up. Hannah Crane reads the letter twice and puts it away in the box that already keeps the town's oldest relic, and answers nothing.

title: The Ros bheag bell raised at Cnoc ghorm
summary: The bell of the old chapel at Ros bheag, carted north at An Dealachadh and crated in a barn for want of a tower to take it, is hung at last in the new church at Cnoc ghorm and rung on a market morning. Its sound carries to the shore road, farther than the town had thought a single bell could reach.

title: The hurdles built on the Muileann fhionn green
summary: The town's carpenters spend most of a month raising pens on the old common green at Muileann fhionn, working from a plan one of them had seen used at a southern fair, to hold the cattle and sheep the new market right will bring down from the hill farms.

title: The first drove south from Muileann fhionn
summary: Hill farmers who had always walked their beasts the long way south now bring them to the new market at Muileann fhionn, and from there the droves go on by the old tracks toward Ceann leathan. Within a few seasons the green stands trodden to mud on every market morning.

title: A young wife of Muileann fhionn keeps her own watch
summary: A woman newly married into Baile chrom from Muileann fhionn, who asked Hannah Crane whether she was not afraid to keep the vigil alone, climbs the headland herself the night it is kept and watches from a careful distance. She tells no one, not even her husband, that she went.

title: Oidhche Glaise kept in the open a second year
summary: Oidhche Glaise is kept in the open on the headland below the light at Baile chrom the year after the bishops' letter and the year after that, on nights Hannah Crane tells no one in advance; no bishop comes north to see for himself what irregular meant.

title: The Cnoc ghorm bell heard on the shore road
summary: On the new church's first market morning the Ros bheag bell in Cnoc ghorm's tower carries out past the fields to the shore road, and carters driving in from Muileann fhionn hear it and know, before they see the tower, that Cnoc ghorm has a church worth the name.
